COPYRIGHT CLAIMS BOARD (CASE ACT, 17 U.S.C. §§ 1501-1511) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Illustration, LLC · A bronze sculpture titled ‘Pacific Light,’ installed in the plaza in 2015.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS COPYRIGHT CLAIMS BOARD INFORMATION SHEET
This Information Sheet describes the Copyright Claims Board, the tribunal that Congress established inside the United States Copyright Office in the Copyright Alternative in Small-Claims Enforcement Act of 2020 (the “CASE Act”), codified at 17 U.S.C. §§ 1501–1511. It is prepared by Jordan T. Reyes for Acme Illustration, LLC concerning A bronze sculpture titled ‘Pacific Light,’ installed in the plaza in 2015. The Copyright Claims Board is an alternative forum that decides a short, closed list of copyright disputes — claims for infringement of an exclusive right under 17 U.S.C. § 106, claims for a declaration of noninfringement, and claims of misrepresentation in a takedown notice or counter notification under 17 U.S.C. § 512(f), together with certain counterclaims and defenses — subject to a ceiling of $30,000 in total monetary recovery in any single proceeding. Proceedings take place through written submissions and internet-based conferences at the offices of the Board rather than through in-person courtroom appearances, a party may appear without a lawyer, and a respondent who is served with a claim may opt out within 60 days, in which case the proceeding is dismissed without prejudice. This document states what Title 17 provides and what two federal district court decisions have said about proceedings before the Board; it is not a claim form, not a filing with the Board or with any court, not a statement of what the Board or a court would do with any dispute concerning A bronze sculpture titled ‘Pacific Light,’ installed in the plaza in 2015., and not legal advice.

HOW THIS INFORMATION SHEET RELATES TO THIS PROJECT'S OTHER COPYRIGHT DOCUMENTS
The Copyright Claims Board is a forum, not a separate body of copyright law, and this Information Sheet does not restate the substantive copyright rules that this project addresses in separate documents. Whether a work or an element of a work is protected at all, and the ideas, facts, and merger and scenes a faire limits on protection, are the subject of this project's document on what copyright does not protect. Fair use, the first sale doctrine, and joint authorship and co-ownership are the subject of separate documents, and 17 U.S.C. § 1504(c)(5) makes a legal or equitable defense under Title 17 or otherwise available under law assertable in a Board proceeding. Registration with the Copyright Office, and the precondition that 17 U.S.C. § 411(a) places on an infringement suit in district court as construed in Fourth Estate Public Benefit Corp. v. Wall-Street.com, are the subject of this project's copyright registration document; 17 U.S.C. § 1505, described in a separate clause of this Information Sheet, states a different registration rule for Board proceedings. The notice-and-takedown machinery of 17 U.S.C. § 512, addressed in this project's DMCA Takedown Notice, DMCA Counter-Notification, and § 512(c) safe harbor documents, connects to this chapter at two points described below: a claim against certain online service providers is noncompliant unless the claimant affirms a prior § 512 notice, and a Board claim can qualify as the court action referred to in § 512(g)(2)(C). This Information Sheet concerning A bronze sculpture titled ‘Pacific Light,’ installed in the plaza in 2015. addresses 17 U.S.C. §§ 1501–1511 only.

THE BOARD: AN ALTERNATIVE FORUM, VOLUNTARY PARTICIPATION, AND APPEARANCE WITHOUT A LAWYER
17 U.S.C. § 1502(a) establishes the Copyright Claims Board in the Copyright Office and describes it as an alternative forum in which parties may voluntarily seek to resolve certain copyright claims regarding any category of copyrighted work. Section 1502(b)(1) provides for 3 full-time Copyright Claims Officers, recommended by the Register of Copyrights and appointed by the Librarian of Congress, and § 1502(b)(2) provides for not fewer than 2 full-time Copyright Claims Attorneys; under § 1503(a)(2)(B) those attorneys provide assistance to members of the public with respect to the procedures and requirements of the Board. Section 1504(a) states that participation is voluntary and that the right of any party to instead pursue a claim, counterclaim, or defense in a district court of the United States, any other court, or any other forum, and to seek a jury trial, is preserved. Section 1506(c) provides that proceedings are conducted at the offices of the Board without the requirement of in-person appearances and take place by means of written submissions, hearings, and conferences carried out through internet-based applications and other telecommunications facilities. Section 1506(d) provides that a party may be, but is not required to be, represented, and identifies the two categories of permitted representatives: an attorney, or a qualified law student providing the representation on a pro bono basis.

THE CLAIMS, COUNTERCLAIMS, AND DEFENSES THE BOARD MAY DECIDE
17 U.S.C. § 1504(c) lists what the Copyright Claims Board may decide, subject to such further limitations and requirements, including with respect to particular classes of works, as the Register of Copyrights sets by regulation. Paragraph (1) covers a claim for infringement of an exclusive right under 17 U.S.C. § 106, brought by the legal or beneficial owner of that right at the time of the infringement, for damages within the monetary limits of § 1504(e)(1). Paragraph (2) covers a claim for a declaration of noninfringement, consistent with the federal Declaratory Judgment Act, 28 U.S.C. § 2201. Paragraph (3) covers a claim under 17 U.S.C. § 512(f) for misrepresentation in connection with a notification of claimed infringement or a counter notification, with remedies limited to those available under chapter 15. Paragraph (4) permits a counterclaim asserted solely against the claimant that arises under § 106 or § 512(f) out of the same transaction or occurrence, or that arises under an agreement pertaining to that same transaction or occurrence if the agreement could affect the relief awarded. Paragraph (5) permits a legal or equitable defense under Title 17 or otherwise available under law, and paragraph (6) permits multiple claims by or against multiple parties only if all claims in the proceeding arise out of the same allegedly infringing activity or continuous course of infringing activities and do not in the aggregate exceed the monetary limits of § 1504(e)(1). Section 1504(f) provides that parties may be found jointly and severally liable if all such parties and relevant claims or counterclaims arise from the same activity or activities.

CLAIMS THE BOARD MAY NOT DECIDE
17 U.S.C. § 1504(d) lists four categories of claims and counterclaims that are not subject to determination by the Copyright Claims Board. The first is any claim or counterclaim that is not a permissible claim or counterclaim under § 1504(c). The second is a claim or counterclaim that has been finally adjudicated by a court of competent jurisdiction, or that is pending before such a court, unless that court has granted a stay to permit the claim to proceed before the Board. The third is a claim or counterclaim by or against a Federal or State governmental entity. The fourth is a claim or counterclaim asserted against a person or entity residing outside of the United States, except where that person or entity initiated the Board proceeding and is subject to counterclaims under chapter 15. Separately, 17 U.S.C. § 1506(f)(3) directs the Board to dismiss a claim or counterclaim without prejudice, on review or at any other time in the proceeding, if the Board concludes that it is unsuitable for determination by the Board, and gives three examples: the failure to join a necessary party, the lack of an essential witness, evidence, or expert testimony, and the determination of a relevant issue of law or fact that could exceed either the number of proceedings the Board could reasonably administer or its subject matter competence.

SECTION 1505: THE REGISTRATION REQUIREMENT FOR INFRINGEMENT CLAIMS BEFORE THE BOARD
17 U.S.C. § 1505(a) provides that an infringement claim or counterclaim may not be asserted before the Copyright Claims Board unless the legal or beneficial owner has first delivered a completed application, a deposit, and the required fee for registration to the Copyright Office, and a registration certificate has either been issued or has not been refused. Section 1505(b) makes a claimant or counterclaimant who has met those requirements eligible to recover actual damages and profits or statutory damages, subject to three conditions: the Board may not render a determination until a registration certificate has been issued, submitted to the Board, and made available to the other parties, who must have an opportunity to address it; a proceeding that cannot go forward because a certificate is pending is held in abeyance, and if the abeyance lasts more than 1 year the Board may, after written notice and 30 days for the parties to respond, dismiss the proceeding without prejudice; and if the Board receives notice that registration has been refused, the proceeding is dismissed without prejudice. Section 1505(c) applies the presumption of 17 U.S.C. § 410(c) in a Board proceeding where the certificate shows registration was issued not later than 5 years after first publication. Section 1505(d) directs the Register of Copyrights to establish regulations allowing the Copyright Office to decide, on an expedited basis, whether to issue or deny registration for an unregistered work at issue before the Board.

THE THREE-YEAR LIMITATIONS PERIOD AND TOLLING OF THE COURT DEADLINE
17 U.S.C. § 1504(b)(1) provides that a proceeding may not be maintained before the Copyright Claims Board unless it is commenced, in accordance with 17 U.S.C. § 1506(e), not later than 3 years after the claim accrued. Section 1504(b)(2) provides that, subject to § 1507(a), a proceeding commenced before the Board tolls the time permitted under 17 U.S.C. § 507(b) — the three-year limitations period for a civil action under the Copyright Act — for commencement of an action on the same claim in a district court of the United States, during the period in which the Board proceeding is pending. Commencement for this purpose is defined by § 1506(e) as the filing of a claim with the Board that includes a statement of material facts, is certified under § 1506(y)(1), and is accompanied by the filing fee prescribed by regulation.

FILING A CLAIM, COMPLIANCE REVIEW, AND THE 90-DAY SERVICE DEADLINE
Under 17 U.S.C. § 1506(e), a proceeding is commenced by filing a claim with the Copyright Claims Board that includes a statement of material facts in support of the claim, is certified under § 1506(y)(1), and is accompanied by a filing fee in the amount prescribed by regulations established by the Register of Copyrights. Section 1506(f)(1) provides for review by a Copyright Claims Attorney: if the claim complies, the claimant is notified and instructed to proceed with service; if it does not, the claimant is notified of the deficiency and permitted to file an amended claim within 30 days without an additional filing fee, with a second 30-day opportunity if the refiled claim is still deficient, and dismissal without prejudice if it remains noncompliant. Section 1506(f)(1)(C)(i) adds a special rule for claims against online service providers: a claim for infringement by reason of storage of, or referral or linking to, infringing material that may be subject to the § 512(b), (c), or (d) liability limitations is considered noncompliant unless the claimant affirms that it previously notified the service provider under the applicable § 512 notice provision and the provider failed to remove or disable access to the material expeditiously. Section 1506(g) then requires the claimant, not later than 90 days after receiving notification to proceed with service, to file proof of service on the respondent; service is effected by personal service or pursuant to a waiver of personal service, as prescribed by regulation, and § 1506(g)(9) provides that service of a claim and waiver of personal service may only be effected within the United States.

THE RESPONDENT'S 60-DAY OPT-OUT RIGHT AND PREEMPTIVE OPT-OUT BY LIBRARIES AND ARCHIVES
17 U.S.C. § 1506(i) gives a respondent who has been properly served with a notice and claim a period of 60 days, beginning on the date of service, to provide written notice to the Copyright Claims Board that the respondent opts out. WHAT A BOARD DETERMINATION DOES AND DOES NOT DECIDE
17 U.S.C. § 1507(a) provides that a final determination, including a default determination or one based on a failure to prosecute, precludes relitigation of the claims and counterclaims actually asserted and finally determined, but only as between the parties to that determination, and subject to three qualifications: it does not preclude litigation of the same or similar issues in connection with claims not asserted or not finally determined; a determination of ownership of a copyrighted work has no preclusive effect in any other action or proceeding; and, except as § 1507 and § 1508 permit, a determination may not be cited or relied upon as legal precedent in any other action or proceeding, including before the Board itself. Section 1507(c) provides that submissions and statements made in a Board proceeding, including a dismissed proceeding, generally may not be cited, relied upon, or serve as the basis of another action concerning rights under Title 17. Section 1507(e) provides that the failure or inability to assert a counterclaim before the Board does not preclude asserting it later in court or in another Board proceeding, and § 1507(f) provides that a party who timely opts out under § 1506(i), or who is dismissed before a final determination issues, is not bound and the determination has no preclusive effect as to that party. Section 1507(d) provides that certain Board claims qualify as an action seeking an order to restrain a subscriber from infringing activity under 17 U.S.C. § 512(g)(2)(C) if notice of the proceeding reaches the service provider's designated agent before the material is replaced and the claim alleges infringement of the material identified in the takedown notification. Section 1509(a) requires a district court to stay proceedings, or grant other appropriate relief, as to a claim already the subject of a pending or active Board proceeding, and § 1509(b) makes a Board proceeding an alternative dispute resolution process under 28 U.S.C. § 651 for referral of eligible cases on the parties' consent.

SECTION 1508(A): TURNING AN UNPAID BOARD AWARD INTO A COURT JUDGMENT
The Copyright Claims Board issues determinations; it does not execute on them. 17 U.S.C. § 1508(a) provides that where a party has failed to pay damages, or otherwise to comply with the relief awarded in a final determination — including a default determination or one based on a failure to prosecute — the aggrieved party may apply, not later than 1 year after the later of the determination, the resolution of any reconsideration or Register review, or the issuance of an amended final determination, to the United States District Court for the District of Columbia or another appropriate district court for an order confirming the relief and reducing the award to judgment. The court is directed to grant such an order and direct entry of judgment unless the determination is or has been vacated, modified, or corrected under § 1508(c), and to impose on the noncomplying party the reasonable expenses required to secure the order, including attorneys' fees, incurred by the aggrieved party. Section 1508(b) requires notice of the application to all parties to the Board proceeding in accordance with the procedures for service of a motion in that district court, a certified copy of the final or amended final determination, and a declaration under penalty of perjury covering the accuracy of the copy, the date of the determination, the basis for any challenge under § 1508(c)(1), and any other proceedings concerning the same determination. expectedJSON.body: The Copyright Claims Board issues determinations; it does not execute on them. 17 U.S.C. § 1508(a) provides that where a party has failed to pay damages, or otherwise to comply with the relief awarded in a final determination — including a default determination or one based on a failure to prosecute — the aggrieved party may apply, not later than 1 year after the later of the determination, the resolution of any reconsideration or Register review, or the issuance of an amended final determination, to the United States District Court for the District of Columbia or another appropriate district court for an order confirming the relief and reducing the award to judgment. The court is directed to grant such an order and direct entry of judgment unless the determination is or has been vacated, modified, or corrected under § 1508(c), and to impose on the noncomplying party the reasonable expenses required to secure the order, including attorneys' fees, incurred by the aggrieved party. Section 1508(b) requires notice of the application to all parties to the Board proceeding in accordance with the procedures for service of a motion in that district court, a certified copy of the final or amended final determination, and a declaration under penalty of perjury covering the accuracy of the copy, the date of the determination, the basis for any challenge under § 1508(c)(1), and any other proceedings concerning the same determination. In In re Bronner v. Essayzoo, the District Court for the District of Columbia applied these provisions to a Board default determination awarding $1,200 in statutory damages, found the § 1508(a) and § 1508(b) requirements satisfied where the movant had served the motion by mail to the respondent's last known address and had filed a certified copy of the determination with a supporting declaration, granted the motion, and imposed the movant's $52 filing cost on the respondent.

expectedJSON.body: 17 U.S.C. § 1503(g) provides that actions of the Copyright Claims Officers and the Register of Copyrights in connection with rendering a determination are subject to judicial review as provided under § 1508(c) and not under chapter 7 of title 5, the judicial review provisions of the Administrative Procedure Act. Section 1508(c)(1) allows a party, not later than 90 days after the later of a final or amended final determination and the completion of any reconsideration or review by the Register, to seek an order from a district court vacating, modifying, or correcting the determination in three cases: where the determination issued as a result of fraud, corruption, misrepresentation, or other misconduct; where the Board exceeded its authority or failed to render a final determination concerning the subject matter at issue; and, in the case of a default determination or a determination based on a failure to prosecute, where it is established that the default or failure was due to excusable neglect. Section 1508(c)(2) requires notice of the application to all parties to the Board proceeding and permits a judge to stay enforcement proceedings while the challenge is pending. In Santora v. Copyright Claims Board, the District Court for the District of Columbia stated that judicial review of the Board's proceedings is governed by the CASE Act, described those three grounds as the only cases in which the court may vacate, modify, or correct a determination, and dismissed a pro se complaint that alleged irregularities in a Board proceeding — which the Board had dismissed for failure to prosecute — without identifying a final or amended final determination and facts satisfying § 1508(c).

expectedJSON.body: 17 U.S.C. § 1506(y)(2) provides that where a determination is rendered and it is established that a party pursued a claim, counterclaim, or defense for a harassing or other improper purpose, or without a reasonable basis in law or fact, the Copyright Claims Board shall, unless inconsistent with the interests of justice, award reasonable costs and attorneys' fees to an adversely affected party in an amount of not more than $5,000. Two exceptions follow: where the adversely affected party appeared pro se, the award is for costs only in an amount of not more than $2,500; and in extraordinary circumstances, such as a demonstrated pattern or practice of bad faith conduct, the Board may award costs and fees in excess of those limits in the interests of justice. Section 1506(y)(3) adds that a party found to have pursued a claim, counterclaim, or defense for a harassing or other improper purpose, or without a reasonable basis in law or fact, on more than one occasion within a 12-month period is barred from initiating a claim before the Board for 12 months from the date of that finding, and any proceeding that party has pending is dismissed without prejudice, except that an active proceeding is dismissed on this basis only with the respondent's written consent. Section 1506(y)(1) directs the Register of Copyrights to establish regulations requiring certification of the accuracy and truthfulness of statements made by participants.
